Hi, Matthieu. I am cc-ing the Stan crew and also Matt Schofield, a colleague who works on these sorts of models. Thanks much.
Andrew

On Jul 7, 2012, at 8:39 AM, Matthieu Authier wrote:

> Dear Prof. Gelman,
>
> I apologize for maybe bothering you with this but I haven't been able to find out which person to contact about contributing an example for Stan.
>
> I did my phD on Southern Elephant Seals, a large marine mammals with an asynchronous breeding biology. Females come ashore to give birth to single pup and wean it within 3 weeks. However, female hauling-out last for 2 months : the total number of females is thus not directly observable.
>
> The hauling-out process in this species has been described with a 4-parameters non-linear model :
>
> the number of females present on day t, N(t) is modelled as:
> N(t) = Ntot x p(t,mu,sigma,S) where p() is a proportion
> p(mu,sigma,S) = phi((t-mu)/sigma) - phi((t-mu-S)/sigma) where phi() is the standard normal cdf
> mu is the peak return date of females
> sigma is the synchrony of females
> S is the average numbers of day needed by a female to wean its pup
>
> To estimate Ntot, mu and sigma, I used a hierarchical model on data collected on 15 harems during 2008 and 2009 on Kerguelen Islands. The data are daily census of the number of females ashore. S was fixed to 28 days. The data were collected by some 18 field workers.
> The parameters (Ntot, mu and sigma) were modelled with a tri-variate normal distribution. Because the correlation between those parameters were of inferential interest, I tried three covariance matrix modelling strategies: (1) Wishart, (2) a Cholesky decomposition and (3) the SVD decomposition of Tokuda et al (2011). All models were fitted with BUGS.
>
> If you feel that this example is interesting enough, I would be very happy to provide the data and code.
> Yours sincerely,
>
> Matthieu

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Contributing an example to Stan
parts:
Matthieu:

Sorry about not being clearer on the home page about who
to contact. We should have an e-mail account for Stan
itself where users can send mail without registering for our
newsgroups.

We were really hoping to get people to contribute working
Stan code, not just model definitions. I should also make
that clearer.

We just don't have the time to port user models. At least
not at the moment. We are happy to help with Stan issues,
of course.

All of what you mention should be codable in Stan, though
I'm not sure what you mean by Cholesky and SVD-based covariance
priors. For instance, we use the Cholesky decomposition as a
step in our Wishart implementation and in our covariance prior
based on Lewandowski et al.

- Bob Carpenter

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Contributing an example to Stan
parts:
We're all ready to go on the Stan site.

For BUGS-size data sets, we should have no problem hosting
them on Google Code. We can also link out, but that tends
to erode over time, so I'd rather not if we don't have to.

What kind of legal ramifications are you worried about, Ben?
I see potential issues with

(a) hosting data we don't have a right to, and

(b) using models that are somehow copyright or patent
encumbered.

I don't see how patent issues are going to be problematic,
but you can run into copyright issues with people contributing
group work they don't own sole copyrights to.

Linking out solves these problems.

Or we could get a lawyer...

- Bob

On Monday, July 9, 2012 6:23:19 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
We're all ready to go on the Stan site.

For BUGS-size data sets, we should have no problem hosting
them on Google Code.  We can also link out, but that tends
to erode over time, so I'd rather not if we don't have to.

What kind of legal ramifications are you worried about, Ben?
I see potential issues with

   (a) hosting data we don't have a right to, and

   (b) using models that are somehow copyright or patent
       encumbered.

I don't see how patent issues are going to be problematic,
but you can run into copyright issues with people contributing
group work they don't own sole copyrights to.

Linking out solves these problems.

Links are (probably) the safest way to go, although they will rot. In addition to your a) and b), we probably don't want to put non-Columbia people in a situation where Columbia can claim to have copyright on the code for their models, so in addition to linking out, whatever steps we can take to ensure that this repository is not "part of" stan will be helpful.
Or we could get a lawyer...

Sadly, not the worst idea. I'd guess things will be okay if we just link. But no one should be guessing.

Ben
